comments.text:
3:20 Ooh this is something of a special interest of mine!!

Hydrophobia is a bit of a misnomer, they aren’t afraid of water. They lose the ability to swallow properly. It’s a bit like if you have a horribly sore throat and you feel the urge to cough or swallow, and you avoid it because it hurts. The rabies virus goes further- it causes the throat to spasm when you try to swallow, which can make you really fearful as it feels like you’re unable to control breathing or swallowing.

If you try to swallow right now, then again very quickly, then another time and another time one after the other, you can start to experience the feeling of those spasms. It’s incredibly distressing. The sick person/animal is dehydrated and likely feeling intense thirst, but it’s not as strong as the fear of the pain and trouble breathing with liquid going in and probably bound to go down the wrong tube every time because there’s just no control of that reflex anymore.

Another common misconception is that animals (including humans) get rabies and develop a rage or urge to bite everything around them. But rabies is such a cool and brilliant virus. That misconception doesn’t quite give it the recognition it deserves in my opinion!

Rabies attacks brain tissue and you lose the ability to properly appraise situations. You get anxious, everything starts to seem like a threat. A movement in front of you seems like an attack, and you feel you need to defend yourself. Not helped by the fever and general sickness going on.

Most animals that we think of as risks for having rabies are predator animals, and that’s no coincidence. Predators defend themselves by biting, and they have lots of experience biting and killing for food, so the muscle memory and reflexive moments allow them to “comfortably” rely on attacking and removing the threat when they feel at risk. Predator animals often associated with rabies are often pack animals too, which means that they are likely to spread the virus to same-species animals. Dogs, coyotes, raccoons, cats are all either very social species or so common that it’s likely to see members of their same species often enough to engage in a fight.

Prey animals like rabbits can get rabies, but that’s not something you hear about very often. The reason for that is because prey animals react differently to threats than predator animals. They don’t tend to bite unless essentially forced. If they survive the transmission at all (rabbits are so susceptible to shock, but hypothetically some saliva etc was transmitted), they can experience that intense anxiety and will simply hide and avoid the threats. They’re not likely to spread it because they probably would just burrow somewhere and panic themselves into shock and death.

Humans don’t get the urge to bite each other when infected with rabies. I have a terrible pet peeve about quite a few zombie movies that are based on some mutant rabies virus going around, lolol 

Anyway. Humans, when they feel threatened, have a bunch of options. They can shout and scream and argue, they can try to flee, they can cry and fold into themselves, they can try to bargain and reason their way out of a threatening situation, etc. etc.

With the high fever and malaise, people often just seem anxious and delirious and agitated. Not enraged, not out of control and needing to be strapped down because they’re trying to spit at and bite everyone.

Rabies is so sad to see in any animal. To be clear, I think the virus is brilliant for limiting the ability to swallow so the saliva with the most viral load stays in the mouth, and then creating anxiety that exploits some animals’ tendency to bite when threatened. I think the effects on the animal are devastating and disturbing, and it’s very hard to watch footage of those suffering from it.

I hope anyone with this interest was able to get through this long-ass comment and maybe find some cool facts about a super smart and almost eldritch horror of a virus!

comments.text:
Hi Dr. Mike! Pre vet student and animal enthusiast here, so I’m glad you’re asking these questions instead of assuming like a lot of people. This will be kind of long but for anyone who wants quick answers to some of the questions Dr. Mike asked, here you go:

For the coyotes attacking people thing, it is rare that they attack people but the frequency is increasing as we expand more. For the most part, they mostly target small animals, pets especially. They are also highly adaptable to practically any environment so them living near humans is becoming more problematic. 

Can whales swallow people? No, they cannot. Their throats are way too narrow to actually swallow (think about the size of a grapefruit) and there have been cases of whales accidentally engulfing people, but then spitting them out. 
Edit: a lot of people have said that sperm whales can, and while yes they technically can, they would also spit people right back out. We aren’t their main food source, so ending up in their mouths would be pure accident and they wouldn’t eat you. Thus there are no credible reported cases of a sperm whale swallowing a person. 

Does bear spray work on polar bears? Yes, but they are less likely to leave the area after like other bears, but this is more to do with the wind and environment. It also probably doesn’t help that polar bears are one of few animals that see humans as prey. 

Of course I’m not an expert but I love studying animals and their behavior so I know a lot of this from years of researching on my own from reliable sources. Hope this helped with anyone who had the same questions as Dr. Mike ❤
comments.author: @Pixanxious

comments.text: 0:35 Coyote attacks on humans are very rare. When they do happen, it's usually a pack, and usually done by the larger, less fearful Eastern Coyote ( which may or may not have crossbred with domestic dogs and Canadian gray wolves ). These attacks are typically carried out on smaller, weaker individuals ( children, the elderly, people typically around 5 ft in height or shorter and around 100lbs or less in weight ) if they're of a predatory nature. In other cases, it's usually somebody who has stumbled onto a den with pups. There are only 2 confirmed fatal Coyote attacks in North American history ( a 3 y/o in California, and a 19 y/o woman in Nova Scotia ).
